chunks.heading: Putting groups together
chunks.text: When we add, we put two groups together to find how many there are in all. The sign + means add. The sign = means is equal to. Example: 4 + 2. Start at 4. Count on 2 more: 5, 6. So 4 + 2 = 6.

chunks.heading: Counting on
chunks.text: To add a small number, start at the bigger number and count on. You can use your fingers or a number line. Example: 9 + 3. Start at 9, then count 10, 11, 12.

chunks.heading: Ano ang pangngalan?
chunks.text: Ang pangngalan ay salitang tumutukoy sa ngalan ng tao, bagay, hayop, lugar o pangyayari. Halimbawa: Ana (tao), lapis (bagay), pusa (hayop), paaralan (lugar) at pista (pangyayari).

chunks.heading: Pantangi at pambalana
chunks.text: Ang pangngalang pantangi ay tiyak na ngalan ng tao, bagay, hayop, lugar o pangyayari. Nagsisimula ito sa malaking titik, tulad ng Jose, Maynila at Ilog Pasig. Ang pangngalang pambalana ay pangkalahatang ngalan. Nagsisimula ito sa maliit na titik, tulad ng bata, lungsod at ilog.

chunks.heading: Pagsasanay
chunks.text: Isulat kung pantangi o pambalana ang bawat pangngalan: 1) guro   2) Bulkang Mayon   3) aso   4) Cebu

chunks.heading: Living things
chunks.text: Living things grow. They need food, water and air. They can move on their own, and they can have young ones. Plants, animals and people are living things.

chunks.heading: Non-living things
chunks.text: Non-living things do not grow, do not eat and cannot have young ones. A rock, a chair and a toy car are non-living things. Some non-living things can move, like a ball, but only when something pushes or carries them.

chunks.heading: Activity
chunks.text: Sort these into living or non-living: 1) carabao   2) pencil   3) gumamela plant   4) cloud

chunks.heading: Evaporation
chunks.text: The sun heats the water in seas, rivers and lakes. The water turns into water vapor, a gas we cannot see, and rises into the air. This is called evaporation.

chunks.heading: Condensation
chunks.text: High in the sky the air is cold. The water vapor cools and turns into tiny droplets of water. The droplets come together and form clouds. This is called condensation.

chunks.heading: Precipitation and collection
chunks.text: When the droplets in the clouds become big and heavy, they fall as rain. This is called precipitation. The rain flows into rivers, lakes and seas, or soaks into the ground. This is called collection. Then the cycle starts again.

chunks.heading: Dissimilar fractions
chunks.text: Dissimilar fractions have different denominators, like 1/4 and 1/3. To add them, first find the least common denominator (LCD): the smallest number that both denominators divide into evenly.

chunks.heading: Rename, then add
chunks.text: Rename each fraction using the LCD. Example: 1/4 + 1/3. The LCD of 4 and 3 is 12. 1/4 = 3/12 and 1/3 = 4/12. Then add the numerators and keep the denominator: 3/12 + 4/12 = 7/12.

chunks.heading: Pagtatatag
chunks.text: Itinatag ni Andres Bonifacio ang Katipunan noong Hulyo 7, 1892, sa Tondo, Maynila, matapos ipatapon si Jose Rizal sa Dapitan. Ang buong pangalan nito ay Kataas-taasan, Kagalang-galangang Katipunan ng mga Anak ng Bayan, o KKK.

chunks.heading: Layunin
chunks.text: Layunin ng Katipunan na makamit ang kalayaan ng Pilipinas mula sa Espanya sa pamamagitan ng himagsikan. Si Emilio Jacinto ang tinaguriang Utak ng Katipunan. Siya ang sumulat ng Kartilya ng Katipunan.

chunks.heading: Sigaw sa Pugad Lawin
chunks.text: Noong Agosto 1896, pinunit ng mga Katipunero ang kanilang mga sedula bilang tanda ng pagsisimula ng himagsikan laban sa Espanya.

chunks.heading: Singular subjects
chunks.text: A singular subject takes a singular verb. In the present tense, a singular verb usually ends in -s or -es. Examples: The bird sings. She watches TV.

chunks.heading: Plural subjects
chunks.text: A plural subject takes a plural verb, which has no -s. Examples: The birds sing. They watch TV. Remember that I and you also take the verb with no -s: I sing. You watch.

chunks.heading: Compound subjects and exercise
chunks.text: Two subjects joined by and are plural: Ana and Ben play chess. Exercise: Choose the correct verb. 1) My brother (walk/walks) to school. 2) The children (play/plays) outside. 3) Maria and Jose (dance/dances) well.

chunks.heading: What speed means
chunks.text: Speed tells how fast an object moves. It is the distance traveled divided by the time it took: speed = distance ÷ time.

chunks.heading: Units
chunks.text: If distance is in kilometers (km) and time is in hours (h), speed is in kilometers per hour (km/h). If distance is in meters (m) and time is in seconds (s), speed is in meters per second (m/s). Example: a jeepney travels 30 km in 1 hour, so its speed is 30 km/h.

chunks.heading: Problems
chunks.text: Find the speed. 1) A tricycle travels 12 km in 0.5 hour. 2) A runner covers 100 m in 20 s. 3) A bus travels 180 km in 3 hours.

chunks.heading: Quadratic equations
chunks.text: A quadratic equation has the form ax² + bx + c = 0. To solve it by factoring, write the left side as a product of two binomials.

chunks.heading: Finding the factors
chunks.text: For x² + bx + c, find two numbers whose product is c and whose sum is b. Example: x² + 7x + 10 = 0. The numbers 5 and 2 multiply to 10 and add up to 7, so (x + 5)(x + 2) = 0.

chunks.heading: Zero product property
chunks.text: If (x + 5)(x + 2) = 0, then x + 5 = 0 or x + 2 = 0, so x = -5 or x = -2. Always check your answers by substituting them back into the equation.

chunks.heading: Demand
chunks.text: Ang demand ay ang dami ng produkto o serbisyo na handa at kayang bilhin ng mamimili sa iba't ibang presyo. Ayon sa Batas ng Demand, magkasalungat ang ugnayan ng presyo at quantity demanded: kapag tumaas ang presyo, bumababa ang dami ng gustong bilhin, at kapag bumaba ang presyo, tumataas ito, kung walang ibang nagbabago (ceteris paribus).

chunks.heading: Iba pang salik
chunks.text: Mga salik bukod sa presyo na nakaaapekto sa demand: kita ng mamimili, panlasa, dami ng mamimili, presyo ng kaugnay na produkto, at inaasahan sa hinaharap.

chunks.heading: Halimbawa
chunks.text: Kapag tumaas ang presyo ng isang kilong bigas mula ₱45 hanggang ₱55, mas kaunting kilo ang binibili ng isang pamilya bawat linggo.

chunks.heading: Plates
chunks.text: The lithosphere is broken into large pieces called plates. Plates move slowly, a few centimeters each year. The place where two plates meet is called a plate boundary.

chunks.heading: Divergent and convergent
chunks.text: At a divergent boundary, plates move apart and new crust forms, as in the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. At a convergent boundary, plates move toward each other. When an oceanic plate sinks under another plate, a deep ocean trench forms, like the Philippine Trench.

chunks.heading: Transform
chunks.text: At a transform boundary, plates slide past each other sideways. This can cause strong earthquakes, as along the San Andreas Fault.

chunks.heading: Formula
chunks.text: Simple interest is earned only on the principal. Formula: I = Prt, where P is the principal, r is the annual interest rate written as a decimal, and t is the time in years.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: You save ₱5,000 at 4% simple interest for 2 years. r = 0.04, so I = 5,000 × 0.04 × 2 = ₱400. The maturity value is F = P + I = ₱5,400.

chunks.heading: Exercise
chunks.text: 1) Find the simple interest on ₱10,000 at 5% for 3 years. 2) Find the maturity value in number 1.

chunks.heading: What the mean is
chunks.text: The mean is the average of a set of data. Add all the values, then divide the sum by how many values there are.

chunks.heading: Example
chunks.text: The scores 3, 5 and 7 have a sum of 15. There are 3 values, so the mean is 15 ÷ 3 = 5.

chunks.heading: Exercise
chunks.text: Find the mean of these quiz scores: 8, 6, 9, 7, 10.

chunks.heading: Go foods
chunks.text: Ang Go foods ay nagbibigay ng lakas o enerhiya sa katawan. Halimbawa: kanin, tinapay, kamote at mais.

chunks.heading: Grow foods
chunks.text: Ang Grow foods ay tumutulong sa paglaki at sa pagpapalakas ng kalamnan at buto. Halimbawa: isda, itlog, gatas, manok at munggo.

chunks.heading: Glow foods
chunks.text: Ang Glow foods ay nagpapalusog sa balat at mata at tumutulong labanan ang sakit. Halimbawa: mga prutas at gulay tulad ng papaya, saging, malunggay at kalabasa.

chunks.heading: Ano ang katapatan?
chunks.text: Ang katapatan ay pagsasabi ng totoo at paggawa ng tama kahit walang nakakakita. Ang taong matapat ay pinagkakatiwalaan ng kanyang pamilya, mga kaibigan at guro.

chunks.heading: Mga halimbawa
chunks.text: Mga halimbawa ng katapatan: pagsasauli ng napulot na pitaka, hindi pangongopya sa pagsusulit, at pag-amin sa nagawang pagkakamali.

chunks.heading: Pagninilay
chunks.text: Sumulat ng tatlong pangungusap: Ano ang gagawin mo kung nakita mong nangongopya ang kaibigan mo sa pagsusulit?

chunks.heading: Ang nobela
chunks.text: Ang Noli Me Tangere ay nobelang isinulat ni Jose Rizal at inilathala noong 1887 sa Berlin. Inilalarawan nito ang mga pang-aabuso sa lipunan noong panahon ng mga Espanyol.

chunks.heading: Mga tauhan
chunks.text: Si Crisostomo Ibarra ay binatang nag-aral sa Europa at nais magpatayo ng paaralan sa San Diego. Si Maria Clara ang kasintahan ni Ibarra. Si Padre Damaso ay prayleng mapang-abuso. Si Elias ay bangkerong tumulong kay Ibarra.

chunks.heading: What an ecosystem is
chunks.text: An ecosystem is a community of living things together with the nonliving things around them, all acting on one another in one place. A pond is an ecosystem. So is a forest, a rice field, a coral reef and even a rotting log. An ecosystem can be as small as a puddle or as large as a whole ocean. Scientists study ecosystems by looking at levels. One single living thing is called an organism. All the organisms of one kind living in the same area form a population, like all the carabaos in one barangay. All the populations living in the same area form a community. When we add the water, soil, air and sunlight of that area, we have an ecosystem. The place where an organism normally lives and finds what it needs is its habitat. The habitat of a mudskipper, for example, is a muddy shore. Each organism also has a role in its ecosystem, and that role is called its niche.

chunks.heading: Biotic and abiotic factors
chunks.text: Every ecosystem has two kinds of parts. Biotic factors are the living parts, such as plants, animals, fungi and bacteria. Things that were once alive, such as fallen leaves and dead animals, are often counted with them too. Abiotic factors are the nonliving parts, such as sunlight, water, air, soil, temperature and salt. Abiotic factors decide which organisms can live in a place. Few plants can grow on the floor of a thick forest because very little sunlight reaches the ground. Most freshwater fish die in the sea because the water is too salty for their bodies. Mangrove trees are able to live in salty mud, so they grow where other trees cannot. Biotic factors act on abiotic factors as well. The roots of trees hold the soil in place, and their leaves give shade that keeps the ground cool and damp. When farmers cut down the trees on a hillside, the soil dries out and heavy rain can wash it away.

chunks.heading: Producers
chunks.text: Producers are organisms that make their own food. Green plants are the most familiar producers. They carry out photosynthesis: using the energy of sunlight, they turn water and carbon dioxide into sugar, and they give off oxygen. The sugar is the food that the plant uses to live and grow, and part of it is stored in the leaves, stems, roots, fruits and seeds. In a rice field, the rice plants are the main producers. In the sea, most of the food is made by phytoplankton, which are tiny living things that float near the surface where sunlight can reach them. Seagrass and seaweed are also producers in the sea. Producers are found at the start of almost every food chain, because the energy that nearly all other organisms use was first captured by them from the sun. Without producers, the animals of an ecosystem would soon have nothing to eat, and the air would slowly lose its oxygen.

chunks.heading: Consumers
chunks.text: Consumers are organisms that cannot make their own food, so they must get it by eating other organisms. They are grouped by what they eat. Herbivores eat only plants. A carabao eating grass and a grasshopper chewing a leaf are herbivores. Carnivores eat other animals. A Philippine eagle hunting a flying lemur and a spider catching a fly are carnivores. Omnivores eat both plants and animals. Humans, chickens and rats are omnivores. Consumers are also grouped by their place in the feeding order. A primary consumer eats producers. A secondary consumer eats primary consumers, and a tertiary consumer eats secondary consumers. An animal that hunts and kills another animal is called a predator, and the animal it hunts is the prey. Predators help an ecosystem stay in balance, since they keep the number of prey animals from growing too large. If all the snakes in a rice field were killed, the number of rats would rise and more of the rice would be eaten.

chunks.heading: Decomposers
chunks.text: Decomposers are organisms that break down dead plants, dead animals and animal wastes. Bacteria and fungi are the main decomposers. Mushrooms growing on a dead log are fungi at work: they soften the wood and feed on it, and after some months the log crumbles into soil. Without decomposers, dead things and wastes would pile up on the ground year after year. Decomposers also return nutrients to the soil and water. Nutrients are materials such as nitrogen and phosphorus that plants need in order to grow. The roots of plants take these nutrients back up, and in this way the same materials are used again and again. This is why farmers make compost out of rice straw, vegetable peelings and animal manure. Inside the compost pile, decomposers change the waste into a dark, crumbly material that makes the soil richer. Earthworms and some insects, such as termites, help too, because they chew dead material into smaller pieces that bacteria and fungi can break down faster.

chunks.heading: Food chains and food webs
chunks.text: A food chain shows how energy passes from one organism to the next when one is eaten by another. Each arrow in a food chain points from the food to the eater. For example, in the chain rice plant → rat → snake → eagle, the rice plant is the producer, the rat is the primary consumer, the snake is the secondary consumer and the eagle is the tertiary consumer. Each step in a chain is called a trophic level. In a real ecosystem, most organisms eat more than one kind of food, and most are eaten by more than one kind of animal. A food web is made up of many food chains that are connected to one another. A rice field food web might include rice, grasshoppers, rats, frogs, snakes, spiders and birds. Food webs are more stable than single chains. If the frogs in a field disappear, the snakes can still eat rats. Still, losing one species can affect many others in the web, and sometimes in ways that farmers do not expect.

chunks.heading: Energy pyramid
chunks.text: An energy pyramid shows how much energy is found at each trophic level of an ecosystem. Producers form the wide bottom of the pyramid because they hold the most energy. Only about 10 percent of the energy at one level passes to the next level. The other 90 percent or so is used by the organism for moving, breathing and keeping warm, or is lost as heat and in wastes. This is called the 10 percent rule. Suppose the grass in a field holds 10,000 units of energy. The grasshoppers that eat it get only about 1,000 units. The frogs that eat those grasshoppers get about 100 units, and the snakes that eat those frogs get about 10 units. Because so little energy reaches the top, an ecosystem can feed many grasshoppers but only a few snakes and even fewer eagles. It also explains why food chains are short, with rarely more than four or five levels. There is simply not enough energy left to support another level above.

chunks.heading: Relationships between organisms
chunks.text: Organisms that live closely together can affect each other in different ways. A close, long-term relationship between two different kinds of organisms is called symbiosis. There are three main types. In mutualism, both organisms benefit. Bees get nectar from a flower, and at the same time they carry pollen that helps the plant make seeds. In commensalism, one organism benefits while the other is neither helped nor harmed. An orchid growing on the branch of a tall tree gets a higher place with more sunlight, and the tree is not hurt. In parasitism, one organism, the parasite, benefits while the other, the host, is harmed. Head lice feed on the blood of a person, and tapeworms live in the intestines of animals and take their food. Organisms also compete. Competition happens when two organisms need the same limited thing, such as food, water, light or space. Young trees in a thick forest compete for sunlight, and the ones that grow too slowly die in the shade.

chunks.heading: Philippine ecosystems
chunks.text: The Philippines has many kinds of ecosystems. Tropical rainforests grow on many of our mountains. They receive heavy rain and hold a very large number of species, including the Philippine eagle and the tarsier. Mangrove forests grow along muddy, salty shores. Their tangled roots trap mud and slow down big waves, which helps to protect coastal towns during storms, and young fish and crabs hide among them. Seagrass beds grow in shallow water and feed sea turtles and dugongs. Coral reefs are built up over many years by tiny animals called coral polyps, which live together in large groups. Reefs give food and shelter to thousands of kinds of fish. The Tubbataha Reefs in the Sulu Sea are a protected area and a World Heritage Site. Lakes and rivers such as Laguna de Bay and the Cagayan River are freshwater ecosystems that give people fish and water. Rice terraces and rice fields are ecosystems shaped by people, yet they still shelter many frogs, birds and insects.

chunks.heading: Threats, conservation and review
chunks.text: Human activities can damage ecosystems. Cutting down forests destroys habitats and leads to soil erosion and floods. Dynamite fishing kills coral reefs along with the fish. Plastic and other wastes clog rivers and harm sea animals that mistake them for food. Too much fertilizer washes into lakes and causes algae to grow out of control, and when the algae die and rot, the water loses its oxygen and fish die. A species brought in from another place, called an invasive species, can crowd out native species. The golden apple snail, brought into the country for food, became a serious pest in rice fields. People can protect ecosystems by planting native trees and mangroves, setting up protected areas, reducing waste and fishing in ways that allow fish to grow back. Review questions: 1) In the chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, which organism is the producer? 2) If the grass holds 5,000 units of energy, about how many units reach the frog? 3) A remora fish rides on a shark and eats its scraps, and the shark is not harmed. What type of symbiosis is this?

chunks.heading: What a ratio is
chunks.text: A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind. If a basket holds 3 mangoes and 5 bananas, the ratio of mangoes to bananas is 3 to 5. We can write this ratio in three ways: in words as 3 to 5, with a colon as 3:5, or as a fraction, 3/5. The order of the numbers matters. The ratio of bananas to mangoes is 5:3, and this is not the same as 3:5. The numbers in a ratio are called its terms. The first term is the quantity named first, and the second term is the quantity named second. When we compare two quantities, both must be in the same unit. To compare 2 meters with 50 centimeters, first change the 2 meters into 200 centimeters. The ratio is then 200:50. A ratio can compare a part with another part, like girls to boys in a class. It can also compare a part with the whole, like girls to all the pupils in the class. Always read the problem carefully to see which of these two is being asked.

chunks.heading: Equivalent ratios and lowest terms
chunks.text: Equivalent ratios are ratios that show the same comparison, even though the numbers are different. To get an equivalent ratio, multiply or divide both terms by the same number other than zero. For example, 2:3 is equivalent to 4:6, since both terms of 2:3 were multiplied by 2. It is also equivalent to 10:15, since both terms were multiplied by 5. A ratio is in lowest terms when its two terms have no common factor other than 1. To write a ratio in lowest terms, divide both terms by their greatest common factor, or GCF. Example: to write 16:24 in lowest terms, find the GCF of 16 and 24, which is 8. Divide both terms by 8: 16 ÷ 8 = 2 and 24 ÷ 8 = 3. So 16:24 in lowest terms is 2:3. You can check whether two ratios are equivalent by writing both of them in lowest terms and comparing. If they come out the same, then the ratios are equivalent. You may also use a table of ratios, where each row is found by multiplying both terms by the same number.

chunks.heading: What a proportion is
chunks.text: A proportion is a statement that two ratios are equal. We can write it with an equal sign, as in 1/2 = 4/8, or with colons, as in 1:2 = 4:8, which is read as 1 is to 2 as 4 is to 8. The four numbers in a proportion have names. In a:b = c:d, the outer numbers a and d are called the extremes, and the inner numbers b and c are called the means. There are two kinds of proportion that you will often meet. In a direct proportion, when one quantity increases, the other quantity increases at the same rate. The more kilos of rice you buy, the more you pay. If 2 kilos cost ₱100, then 4 kilos cost ₱200. In an inverse proportion, when one quantity increases, the other quantity decreases. The more workers there are, the fewer days it takes to finish the job. If 2 workers need 6 days to paint a house, then 4 workers working at the same pace need only 3 days. Before you solve a problem, first decide which kind of proportion it is.

chunks.heading: Cross products
chunks.text: In any proportion, the two cross products are equal. For a/b = c/d, this means that a × d = b × c. We can use this to test whether two ratios form a proportion. Example: does 2/3 = 8/12? Multiply across: 2 × 12 = 24 and 3 × 8 = 24. The products are the same, so the two ratios do form a proportion. We can also use cross products to find a missing term. Example: find n in 2/5 = n/30. Step 1: multiply across to get 5 × n = 2 × 30. Step 2: simplify the side that has only numbers, so 5 × n = 60. Step 3: divide both sides by the number beside n, so n = 60 ÷ 5 = 12. Step 4: check your work by putting the number back: 2 × 30 = 60 and 5 × 12 = 60. Word problems work the same way. If 3 notebooks cost ₱75, how much do 7 notebooks cost? Set up 3/75 = 7/n, keeping notebooks on top and pesos below on both sides. Then 3 × n = 75 × 7 = 525, so n = 175, and 7 notebooks cost ₱175.

chunks.heading: What percent means
chunks.text: Percent means per hundred, or out of 100. The symbol for percent is %. So 35% means 35 out of 100, which we may also write as the ratio 35:100 or the fraction 35/100. Imagine a grid of 100 small squares. If 35 of the squares are shaded, then 35% of the grid is shaded, and 65% is not shaded. The whole of anything is 100%. Half of something is 50%, one fourth is 25% and three fourths is 75%. Learning these common percents by heart will make many problems faster. Percent can also be more than 100. If a school had 200 pupils last year and has 300 pupils this year, then this year's number is 150% of last year's number. Percents are used in everyday life. We see them in discounts at the store, in interest on savings in the bank, in taxes, in test scores, and in reports about the weather, such as a 60% chance of rain. Because a percent is always out of 100, percents make it easy to compare things that have different totals.

chunks.heading: Changing between fractions, decimals and percents
chunks.text: A number can be written as a fraction, a decimal or a percent. To change a percent to a decimal, remove the % sign and divide by 100, which moves the decimal point two places to the left. So 45% = 0.45 and 8% = 0.08. To change a decimal to a percent, do the opposite: multiply by 100, which moves the decimal point two places to the right, and then add the % sign. So 0.6 = 60% and 0.125 = 12.5%. To change a percent to a fraction, write the number over 100 and simplify. So 40% = 40/100 = 2/5. To change a fraction to a percent, there are two ways. The first way works when the denominator can easily become 100. For 3/20, multiply both terms by 5 to get 15/100, which is 15%. The second way always works: divide the numerator by the denominator to get a decimal, and then change the decimal to a percent. For 3/8, we divide 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375, and this is 37.5%.

chunks.heading: Finding the percentage
chunks.text: Most percent problems have three parts. The base (B) is the whole amount, the rate (R) is the number with the percent sign, and the percentage (P) is the part of the whole. The three parts are related by P = R × B. Before you multiply, change the rate to a decimal or a fraction. Example: find 30% of 150. The base is 150 and the rate is 30%, which is 0.30. So P = 0.30 × 150 = 45. The word of in a percent problem usually tells you to multiply. Sometimes a fraction is easier than a decimal. To find 50% of a number, take half of it. To find 25% of a number, divide it by 4. To find 10% of a number, move the decimal point one place to the left. So 10% of 90 is 9, and then 20% of 90 is two times that, or 18. Word problem: a class has 40 pupils, and 15% of them walk to school. How many walk? P = 0.15 × 40 = 6, so 6 pupils walk to school. Always label your answer with the correct unit.

chunks.heading: Finding the rate and the base
chunks.text: When the percentage and the base are given, we can find the rate with R = P ÷ B. Write the answer as a percent. Example: 12 is what percent of 48? R = 12 ÷ 48 = 0.25, so the rate is 25%. Word problem: a pupil got 18 items right out of 24 on a quiz. What was the score in percent? R = 18 ÷ 24 = 0.75, so the score was 75%. When the percentage and the rate are given, we can find the base with B = P ÷ R. Example: 9 is 15% of what number? B = 9 ÷ 0.15 = 60. Check your work by multiplying: 15% of 60 is 0.15 × 60 = 9. Word problem: there are 14 girls in a club, and they make up 35% of the members. How many members does the club have? B = 14 ÷ 0.35 = 40, so the club has 40 members. To decide which formula to use, write down what the problem gives you first. The missing part tells you which formula you need. A common mistake is to use the percentage as the base, so be careful to find which number stands for the whole.

chunks.heading: Discount and sale price
chunks.text: Stores often lower their prices by a percent. The original price is the price before the sale, and it is the base. The discount rate is the percent taken off. The discount is the amount of money you save. To find the discount, multiply: discount = discount rate × original price. To find the sale price, subtract: sale price = original price − discount. Example: a pair of shoes costs ₱800, and the store gives a 20% discount. The discount is 0.20 × 800 = ₱160. The sale price is 800 − 160 = ₱640. There is a shortcut. If 20% is taken off, you still pay 80% of the price, and 0.80 × 800 is also ₱640. We can find a discount rate as well. A shirt that used to cost ₱250 is now on sale for ₱200. The amount saved is 250 − 200 = ₱50, and the rate is 50 ÷ 250 = 0.20, or 20%. Compare carefully when shopping. A big discount on an expensive item may still cost more than a small discount on a cheaper one. Remember that the rate is always taken from the original price and not from the sale price.

chunks.heading: Exercises
chunks.text: Solve each problem in your notebook and show your solution. Exercise 1: Write the ratio 12:18 in lowest terms. Exercise 2: Find x in the proportion 3/4 = x/20. Exercise 3: If 5 pencils cost ₱40, how much do 8 pencils cost? Exercise 4: Find 25% of 80. Exercise 5: A pupil answered 21 items correctly out of 30. What is the score in percent? Exercise 6: 30 is what percent of 120? Exercise 7: 16 is 20% of what number? Exercise 8: A bag costs ₱400, and the store gives a 15% discount. What is the sale price of the bag? Exercise 9: Six out of 24 mangoes in a basket are ripe. What percent of the mangoes are ripe? Exercise 10: Write 3/5 as a percent. Bonus: A barangay had 500 families last year and has 600 families this year. This year's number is what percent of last year's number? When you finish, check each answer by putting it back into the problem. Ask your teacher about any item you are unsure of, and try a similar problem on your own for practice.
